metaTitle: The white bear invites you to... advertise on social media
metaDescription: Can the viral about the costumed bear in Zakopane teach us anything about social media? A note on paying for reach.

runs.text: The clip of the costumed bear in Zakopane, Poland's best-known mountain resort, demanding a fee for the use of its image echoed all across the internet, and countless real-time marketing posts flooded Monday's social feeds, our client's included:
Source: a post by the Vobis.pl brand on Facebook

The whole thing got us thinking, though: those photos with the bear look a bit like… working in social media. Setting aside the intentions of the woman who filmed it, who in this case had no interest in a photo with the mascot at all, the point of pictures like that is usually to show off, among friends or on your own profile, an interesting piece of the folklore of Krupówki, the town's main drag. For a brand publishing on Facebook/Instagram/LinkedIn or anywhere else, the point is to show interesting pieces of its own backyard.

And how do the algorithms on those platforms behave here? Much the same way. Want to show off your content? Pay for an ad. Just as the bear charges for a photo, social platforms charge to effectively put your posts in front of an audience.
Don't pay and you won't show your friends the photo.
Don't pay and you won't show your audience what matters to you.

Sometimes, of course, you get away with it off the books. The bear in question won't notice you snapped a photo without paying, and every so often the algorithm lets through a post with very strong organic numbers. As a rule, though, the same principle governs both cases: pay to get a result.

Walking the streets of Zakopane, we'll be told that a photo with the bear is an absolutely unmissable souvenir from the capital of the Polish mountains. Posting something, we'll be told that even a modest promotion will get us in front of a wide audience.

The two situations differ in exactly one way, and unfortunately it's the one that counts against everyone working in social media: skip paying the bear and the trip will probably still be a great one, and our memories won't feel the loss. Skip paying that social media bear, though, and all the preparation goes to waste, leaving us with the bitterness of a goal we didn't hit.
